question:
A 52-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with sudden right scrotal pain, accompanied
by swelling and nausea, which began three hours earlier after lifting a heavy object. He reports that the
swelling has been intermittently present for years, worsening with physical strain or coughing, but it had
never been painful before. His medical history is unremarkable, but he has a 26-pack-year smoking
history. Vital signs include blood pressure of 159/86 mm Hg, heart rate of 85/min, respiratory rate of
15/min, and temperature of 37.8■ (100.0■). BMI is 32.9 kg/m2. Physical examination reveals a
moderately distended abdomen and a tender, erythematous, non-reducible scrotal swelling on the
right. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis in this patient? Answer
Choices: (A) Ultrasonography (B) Exploratory laparoscopy (C) No further tests are needed (D) Scrotal
transillumination (E) Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum (F) Testicular biopsy (G) Complete blood count
(CBC) (H) MRI of the scrotum (I) CT scan (J) Abdominal X-ray
 A. Scrotal transillumination
B. Testicular biopsy
C. Abdominal X-ray
D. Ultrasonography
E. CT scan
F. Complete blood count (CBC)
G. Exploratory laparoscopy
H. MRI of the scrotum
I. Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum
J. No further tests are needed
